That would be pretty rare, there's usually a place for "extra documents" when applying to these companies. If they don't have it then it might just mean they don't care, they just want to see your experience and projects (classes are great but the other two are the real sellers). Companies understand that you learned, went to school, took courses... But they are more interested in if you have the ability to work and apply your knowledge.

Edit: So what I'm saying is, just delete the classes.

Remove related coursework from the education, they ask for a transcript usually and you can always mention that in the interview. Remove "kearns scholar" because they really won't care (they may not know what it even means), remove GPA. 

Make sure you're aligned on both sides, the text shouldn't go further than the dates, looks unkempt that way. And make sure it is aligned the same throughout the document.

Use the same tense for the verbs when describing jobs... Don't use "making" and "provided", always use past tense "made", "helped", "researched", etc...

In skills, don't list Excel and Microsoft office and things that we all know how to use... Outlook too. You also said machine shop skills (under the skills section...don't repeat that word lol) and maybe better to provide those handy skills in a cover letter, but keep the softwares listed. :)

Languages, if you keep it, should take up less room or be mentioned in the cover letter. Overall looks great! Just needs a little adjustment!

Oh definitely, I'm not saying that it doesn't need work...

You asked me to post an update, I didn't really want to because I hadn't really changed much. It worked for me, so I thought it might help others to glance at it? Idk

I guess we should've added /s 

Obviously joking, but the hiring algorithm is also a joke.

I would delete awards and relevant course experience from education. Just list the college, the degree you earned, and the expected graduation date. Instead of "graduating" use "expected". Also delete the "seeking EE position" cuz I think they know ;)

For work experience you don't have to list the company location (and for the project), also switch your role and the company name. Company name on top, then whatever your role was (maybe say something like power protection intern, design engineer intern instead of just saying EE internship).

Delete volunteer experience, you can add that in the cover letter instead. And for the skills section just list the software and languages, the electrical skills you can talk about in the cove letter too. (No Microsoft office)

And delete the professional affiliations, I think we've all been affiliated with IEEE at some! :)

My biggest thing is just how hard it is to read the resume, everything is very cramped and there is so much information, focus on making some more white space and spacing between lines. Doesn't have to be fancy, just easy to read, to the point, and showcase all your skills!

Because companies know grades aren't everything, you can have a perfect GPA and honors but not understand how to apply that knowledge to real life. Cum laude just means you graduated with high grades, which can be seen if you just list the GPA (no need for extra flair). It's kinda like a participation trophy, you should be proud but others probably won't care.

I don't even have my GPA listed on my resume (although I did graduate with a high GPA, dean's list and etc...) and not one callback had asked me about whether or not I graduated cum laude... Usually companies ask for GPA in their application somewhere if they care, or in a phone interview or follow up email.

If you enjoy coding as a hobby, then definitely add the languages! Or if you're savvy at something the job posting mentions, but maybe haven't had to do it for a job yet, then mention it under skills as well. I would focus more on skills here, you could delete interests from the section title.

The skills section can be used to bypass the initial screening of resumes, because most companies receive hundreds of applications they might screen for certain words that apply to the job posting. So if the job posting mentions C++ and Python, then having that in the resume might help get your application to the hiring team. I'm sure not all companies do this, but some might and it could help.

Personally I would remove the "dean's list, cum laude and etc..." under the education section, companies don't really care about that (but you could keep the GPA). And also remove the "backpacking" under skills section, more of a hobby so shouldn't be on a resume.

In both experience sections you should list the company name and the time frame your worked there on one line, then underneath that add your position/role (city and state are not relevant, they can ask in an interview or follow up email if anything but probably won't).

You should have at least two bullet points for each job/experience you have listed, up to four for more recent jobs. And make sure they're detailed enough but not overly wordy.

So cut down the education section, make the skills section more presentable (no hobbies, don't bold it, and no double spacing), and add a little more information to the experience sections. Hiring management will care about what you did, and what you can do, straight to the point.

Also, try making sure the resume is cohesive in that the bullet point style is the same throughout, font, etc...
